inputs.finding: Structurally equivalent. Java and Rust transition labels match family, font-size, textLength, x, and y for both labels.
Structurally equivalent. The fallback from defaultFontName to arrow text uses Courier New and both baselines match Java.
Only known minty pseudostate/background residue appeared in strict diff. Extracted transition-label rows for 'theme then override' and 'stop' matched Java exactly, including y baselines.

The first Arial italic transition label matches Java exactly. The second label y differs by +1px together with downstream node, path, polygon, and canvas y drift, so this is not isolated evidence against the family-baseline mechanism.
Both Arial bold transition labels match Java exactly. The note text baseline differs by 0.3618px and later node/route y values drift, outside this transition-label family-baseline mechanism.

Rejecting counterexample. Java renders the label 'boot pass\nsecond line' as two Display text atoms, 'boot pass' at y=187.4785 and 'second line' at y=201.0723. Rust renders one text element containing the literal backslash-n text 'boot pass\nsecond line' at y=188.4785 with textLength=158.4258. This violates the account's broader Display-model claim and misses a transition-label path requested by the held-out multiline axis.

The label family, size, and textLength match Java, but Rust ignores or diverges on the left-to-right layout in this no-oracle path. This is a direction/layout residue rather than a font-baseline-specific failure.

The label family, size, and textLength match Java for self-link and directional labels, but the solved routing/topology differs substantially. This does not disprove the baseline ascent wiring by itself.

verdict_reason: The narrow single-line transition-label family baseline wiring is supported by controlled Verdana, Courier New, Arial, and minty override cases, and no fixture-shaped implementation logic was found. However, the committed causal account claims the Java Display text-block model and includes multiline labels as a perturbation axis. The fresh valid nested Courier New multiline case disproves that broader claim: Java splits the transition label into two text atoms while Rust emits a literal backslash-n as one label. Under the held-out perturbation rule, this relevant counterexample rejects acceptance until the multiline Display behavior is either fixed or explicitly scoped out by a new causal account and target.
